overview: A pneumatic cylinder produces linear push/pull force from compressed air pressure acting on a piston, and a double-acting cylinder (the common industrial type) can be actively driven in both directions by routing air to either end. The solenoid valve is the electrical-to-pneumatic interface: it doesn't touch the cylinder's air directly with electricity, it just uses a small electromagnet to shift a spool that redirects compressed air from the supply line to one port or the other (and vents the opposite port to exhaust). This is a fundamentally different actuation philosophy from an electric actuator: pneumatics are fast, powerful for their size, and simple to make fail-safe (spring-return valves vent to a known state on power loss), but the system only works with a compressor and air-prep (filter/regulator/lubricator) supplying clean, dry, pressurized air — there's no such thing as a pneumatic cylinder that 'just plugs into a battery.' Precise intermediate positioning is also genuinely harder than with an electric actuator, because air is compressible — a simple on/off valve only gives you two reliable end positions, and true proportional position control needs a proportional valve and pressure feedback, not just a bigger solenoid.
simpleSummary: A cylinder that pushes or pulls using compressed air, switched on and off by a small electric solenoid valve that redirects the airflow.

specifications.forceOutput: Pressure x piston area, e.g. ~480N push at 6 bar on a 32mm bore
specifications.valveType: 5/2-way monostable solenoid valve (5 ports, 2 switching positions, spring-return)
specifications.solenoidVoltage: 24V DC (common), also 12V DC or 110/230V AC variants
specifications.actuationSpeed: Full stroke typically under 1 second, tunable with flow-control (speed) valves
specifications.cushioning: Adjustable pneumatic end-of-stroke cushioning on most industrial cylinders
specifications.requiredSupply: Clean, dry compressed air from a compressor + filter-regulator-lubricator (FRL) unit

pinMap.name: PORT_A
pinMap.function: Cap-end air port — pressurizing this port extends the piston rod.
pinMap.gotcha: Undersized tubing or fittings on this line throttle airflow just like a resistor throttles current — the cylinder will move noticeably slower than its rated speed even though the valve and pressure are both correct.

pinMap.name: PORT_B
pinMap.function: Rod-end air port — pressurizing this port retracts the piston rod.
pinMap.gotcha: The rod-end has less effective piston area than the cap-end (the rod itself takes up space), so retract force and speed are noticeably lower than extend force/speed at the same supply pressure — easy to miss when sizing a lifting application.

pinMap.name: SUPPLY_AIR
pinMap.function: Compressed air inlet to the solenoid valve, fed from the shop air line or compressor through an FRL (filter-regulator-lubricator) unit.
pinMap.gotcha: Skipping the filter/regulator stage lets moisture and particulate into the valve — condensation in the lines is a leading cause of sticky, slow-to-shift solenoid valves in humid environments.

pinMap.name: EXHAUST
pinMap.function: Exhaust port where the valve vents the depressurized side of the cylinder to atmosphere during each stroke.
pinMap.gotcha: A blocked or muffler-restricted exhaust port doesn't stop the cylinder from moving, it just slows it down and can cause pressure to back up — a surprising 'why is this suddenly sluggish' failure mode.

pinMap.name: SOLENOID_COIL+
pinMap.function: Solenoid valve coil terminal — energizing the coil shifts the valve spool to route supply air to the opposite cylinder port.
pinMap.currentLimit: Coil-dependent, typically a few hundred mA at 24V DC
pinMap.gotcha: This coil draws real inductive current and needs a driver (relay/transistor/PLC output) sized for it, plus a flyback diode on DC coils — driving it directly from a microcontroller pin will not work and can damage the pin.

pinMap.name: REED_EXTEND
pinMap.function: Magnetic reed (or Hall) switch mounted in a slot on the cylinder barrel, triggered by the piston's internal magnet when the rod reaches full extension.
pinMap.currentLimit: N/A (sensor output, often needs a pull-up/pull-down)
pinMap.gotcha: These slide-in-a-slot position sensors need to be positioned and locked down precisely against the actual stroke length — a sensor that's a few millimeters out of place reports 'extended' before the rod has actually finished traveling.

pinMap.name: REED_RETRACT
pinMap.function: Magnetic reed/Hall switch triggered at full retraction.

useCases.title: Pick-and-place gripper actuation
useCases.scenario: Extend/retract a pneumatic gripper or pusher on a fast production line, switching the solenoid valve from a PLC output for split-second, repeatable strokes.

useCases.title: Part-present clamping fixture
useCases.scenario: Clamp a workpiece in a jig using cylinder force, confirming full clamp engagement via the extend reed switch before a downstream process (like welding) proceeds.

useCases.title: Fail-safe safety guard
useCases.scenario: Use a spring-return monostable valve so a loss of electrical power automatically vents the cylinder to a known safe (retracted) position, rather than leaving it wherever it was.

useCases.title: High-force stamping/pressing station
useCases.scenario: Use a large-bore cylinder at higher supply pressure to generate stamping force well beyond what an electric linear actuator of similar size could produce.

useCases.title: Cycle-time monitoring
useCases.scenario: Read both reed switches into a PLC or microcontroller to time and verify each extend/retract cycle, flagging a fault if a stroke takes longer than expected (indicating an air leak or worn seal).

commonlyPairedWith: PLC or relay module driving the solenoid coil
Flow-control (speed-control) valves for stroke speed tuning
oftenConfusedWith: linear-actuator (self-contained electric actuator — plugs straight into a DC supply with no compressor, no air lines, and gives native proportional position control; the pneumatic cylinder needs a whole compressed-air system and is fundamentally an on/off, end-to-end actuator without a proportional valve)

solenoid (a small electromagnet that directly snaps a plunger — no compressed air involved at all, despite the shared 'solenoid valve' name using the same electromagnet principle just to shift a valve spool instead)
oftenUpgradedTo: Proportional pneumatic valve with pressure feedback, for true intermediate position control instead of just two end positions

beginnerMistakes: Assuming it can run off a battery like an electric actuator — it needs a compressor and prepared (filtered, regulated) compressed air supply to do anything at all.
Driving the solenoid coil directly from a microcontroller GPIO pin instead of through a relay or transistor driver rated for the coil's real inductive current.
Expecting precise intermediate stopping positions from a simple on/off valve — without a proportional valve and feedback, air's compressibility makes mid-stroke positions unrepeatable.
Forgetting the rod-end has less piston area than the cap-end, so retract force/speed is noticeably lower than extend — a problem when the cylinder is oriented to lift a load on retraction.
Skipping the filter-regulator stage on the air supply, letting moisture into the valve and causing slow, sticky, or intermittent shifting over time.
